meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king'?
meta.ogDescription: Erasmus recorded this ancient proverb in Latin in his 1500 Adagia — he was the compiler, not the author. The English is a translation.

answer.label: Not coined by Erasmus — an ancient proverb he collected
answer.authorDates: Greek/proverbial origin · printed in Latin by Erasmus, 1466–1536
answer.sourceLine: Erasmus really did print this line — as the Latin adage “In regione caecorum rex est luscus” in his ‘Adagia’ (1500) — but his book was a famous collection of classical proverbs, and here he was translating an existing Greek saying. He is the compiler and translator, not the author, and the English wording circulating today is a rendering of his Latin, not words Erasmus himself wrote in English.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Ancient / Greek origin — not coined by Erasmus

source.excerpt:
“In regione caecorum rex est luscus.”
— In the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king.
trail: Erasmus printed the Latin adage “In regione caecorum rex est luscus” in the earliest, 1500 edition of his proverb collection, per Wikipedia’s account of the proverb.
In the same passage he follows and translates a similar Greek proverb into Latin — he is collecting and rendering an existing saying, not inventing one, as Wikipedia notes.
An older Aramaic form — “in the street of the blind, the one-eyed man is called the guiding light” — appears in the Genesis Rabbah (4th–5th c. CE), per Wiktionary’s etymology.
The English wording is a translation; a documented early English variant is George Herbert’s 1640 “In the kingdom of blind men, the one-eyed is king”, cited by Wikipedia.
source.excerptNote: Erasmus lists this alongside a related adage, “Inter caecos regnat strabus” (Among the blind the squinter rules), and follows a similar Greek proverb which he renders into Latin — the mark of a compiler translating an inherited saying, not an original coinage.

source.rightsNote: Both the source and the wording are long out of copyright: Erasmus’ Latin adage was first printed in 1500, and the English proverb has circulated for centuries (George Herbert’s variant dates to 1640) — all far earlier than the 1931 U.S. copyright threshold. The saying is a public-domain proverb, not an in-copyright authored line.

author.name: Desiderius Erasmus
author.heading: Erasmus the collector, not the coiner
author.metaLine: 1466–1536 · Dutch Renaissance humanist & compiler of the Adagia
author.bio: Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam was the leading humanist scholar of the Northern Renaissance, best known for his edition of the Greek New Testament and for ‘The Praise of Folly.’ His ‘Adagia’ — first printed in 1500 and expanded across his life to thousands of entries — was a vast anthology of Greek and Latin proverbs with his commentary. Because so many classical sayings reached modern readers through that anthology, Erasmus is routinely miscredited as the author of proverbs he merely gathered and translated, this one among them.

misattribution.heading: How the credit goes wrong
misattribution.intro: The quote is real and it really is in Erasmus’ work — but the popular “Erasmus said this” label mistakes an anthologist for an author.

items.why: The proverb is older than Erasmus. He was translating a similar Greek saying into Latin, and an earlier Aramaic form appears in the Genesis Rabbah centuries before, per Wiktionary.

Erasmus wrote “In regione caecorum rex est luscus” in Latin. The English “In the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king” is a later translation of that Latin — documented English forms like George Herbert’s 1640 “the one-eyed is king” are collected by Wikipedia.

misattribution.truthLine: What’s true: the Latin adage genuinely appears in Erasmus’ 1500 Adagia — but as a proverb he gathered and translated, not one he authored.

context.heading: Why the mix-up is so common
lead: Erasmus’ ‘Adagia’ did for classical proverbs what a great dictionary does for words: it collected thousands of them in one authoritative place. The unintended side effect is that any saying traceable to the ‘Adagia’ tends to get filed under “Erasmus” — even when Erasmus himself was explicitly quoting the Greeks and Romans before him.

This particular line is a textbook case. The thought is universal and ancient; Erasmus gave it a crisp Latin form; centuries of English writers then re-translated it. The result is a genuine, well-sourced proverb wearing a single author’s name it never really had.
context.pull: A dictionary of proverbs is not the author of the proverbs.
